name: Diphenhydramine / doxylamine sleep aids

card.summary: Over-the-counter sedating antihistamines used for sleep; guideline bodies rate their insomnia evidence poorly and they carry anticholinergic effects.
card.note: Anticholinergic side effects; AASM guideline recommends against use for insomnia.

quick.overview:
Diphenhydramine and the related doxylamine are first-generation antihistamines that cause drowsiness and are the active ingredients in many nonprescription sleep aids. People turn to them for sleep onset, which looksmaxxers link to skin and facial recovery.

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline recommended against diphenhydramine for insomnia, citing poor effectiveness and low-quality evidence.
quick.mechanism: Diphenhydramine is an inverse agonist at histamine H1 receptors and crosses the blood-brain barrier, producing drowsiness. It is also a strong muscarinic antagonist, which explains dry mouth, urinary retention and confusion.
quick.risks: Reported effects include dizziness, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, and at higher doses confusion, hallucinations and delirium; overdose can cause arrhythmia. Anticholinergic drug use in later life has been linked to cognitive decline, though a 2019 study found no significant association for antihistamines specifically.

lead: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl, ZzzQuil, Sominex) and doxylamine (Unisom, the sedating ingredient in NyQuil) are first-generation antihistamines sold over the counter as sleep aids. People in lifting and looksmaxxing circles use them to fall asleep and stay asleep, with the chain being better sleep, then better recovery and training, and a fresher-looking face.[1][2]

Sleep shows on the face. In an experimental study in BMJ, people photographed after sleep restriction were judged less healthy and less attractive by observers, and later work measured changes in skin colour, eye openness, mouth curvature and periorbital darkness after sleep deprivation.[4][5][6] That is the appearance case people make for anything that helps sleep.

Guidance on these drugs for insomnia is cautious. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommended against diphenhydramine for insomnia in 2017, citing low-quality evidence, and a 2022 network meta-analysis found little evidence to guide its use; for doxylamine, the same analysis reported a moderate-certainty benefit over placebo at four weeks and no longer-term data.[1][2]

chain: Sedating antihistamine blocks histamine H1 receptors in the brain
More sleep supports recovery, training and a rested look
angle.text: Users take these products to get to sleep when stress, training or stimulants interfere. The appearance link is sleep itself, which observers rate as healthier and more attractive looking.

paras: Both drugs are used for short-term insomnia. Wikipedia describes doxylamine as one of the most widely used sleep medications in the world, with 25 mg given as the most common sleep-aid strength on product labels.[2] Diphenhydramine is likewise a common ingredient in nonprescription sleep aids, and Wikipedia notes that many such products contain the same active ingredient under different names.[1]

On T Nation, men on testosterone therapy or anabolic cycles who struggle with sleep discuss both drugs. One poster says many sleep aids are simply diphenhydramine in a different box and that its effect wears off in a few hours; another describes doxylamine as stronger and longer acting but with a pronounced next-day hangover.[7][8][9]

Diphenhydramine acts mainly as an inverse agonist at H1 receptors, and its central effects cause drowsiness. It is also a potent muscarinic antagonist, a sodium channel blocker and a weak serotonin reuptake inhibitor.[1] Doxylamine mainly blocks H1 receptors and weakly blocks muscarinic receptors; its oral bioavailability is about 25 percent and peak levels occur 1.5 to 2.5 hours after dosing.[2]

The most common effects are drowsiness, dizziness and poor coordination. Anticholinergic effects include dry mouth, faster heart rate, urinary retention, constipation and blurred vision; higher doses can cause confusion, hallucinations or delirium, and overdose can cause QT prolongation and arrhythmias. Paradoxical excitation occurs, especially in children, and normal doses can aggravate restless legs syndrome.[1]
Doxylamine's long half-life can cause next-day sedation, tolerance can develop, and rebound insomnia can occur after stopping.[2]

Anticholinergic exposure in later life has been linked to cognitive decline and dementia, but a 2019 JAMA Internal Medicine nested case-control study found the strongest associations for other anticholinergic classes and no significantly increased risk for antihistamines.[1]

George Rieveschl and his student Fred Huber discovered diphenhydramine in 1943 at the University of Cincinnati while researching muscle relaxants; it became the first FDA-approved prescription antihistamine in 1946, and in the 1960s its weak serotonin reuptake inhibition helped lead to the development of fluoxetine.[1] Doxylamine was reported by Nathan Sperber and colleagues in 1948 or 1949 and has been NyQuil's antihistamine since 1966; the doxylamine and vitamin B6 combination Bendectin was withdrawn in the US in 1983, and Diclegis was approved in 2013.[2]

Evidence assessments for insomnia are summarised in the 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline, which recommended against diphenhydramine, and in a 2022 network meta-analysis that found little evidence to guide its use of diphenhydramine and a moderate-certainty benefit over placebo at four weeks for doxylamine.[1][2] Older laboratory studies compared sedative effects of antihistamines and measured daytime sleepiness after use.[3][10]
No studies found on appearance outcomes of these drugs. Studies of sleep restriction and facial appearance are described in the lead.[4][5][6]

Diphenhydramine is over-the-counter in the US and Canada, a pharmacy medicine in the UK, and prescription-only in Sweden; it is unscheduled internationally but prohibited in Zambia. FDA labeling since 2002 warns against combining multiple products that contain it.[1]

lore.intro: On T Nation, men dealing with sleep problems during testosterone therapy or training compare OTC sleep aids and swap experiences.[7][8][9]

claims.claim: Doxylamine is the strongest OTC sleep aid and carries a heavy hangover.
claims.believers: A poster calls doxylamine the strongest over-the-counter option, as found in Unisom, working very well but leaving them sleepy for two to three days.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports doxylamine's half-life of 7 to 15 hours and notes next-day sedation as a known effect.[2]

claims.claim: Diphenhydramine wears off after a few hours and wakes you mid-night.
claims.believers: Posters say its effect lasts only four to five hours and that dry eyes and nose can follow.[7][9][11]
claims.experts: Guidance bodies have rated diphenhydramine's insomnia evidence poorly and the drug has anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and blurred vision.[1]

claims.claim: Antihistamine sleep aids can be used nightly to build a sleep pattern.
claims.believers: One poster describes taking it repeatedly to condition a sleep pattern.[9]
claims.experts: The AASM has not recommended OTC antihistamines for chronic insomnia, citing a lack of efficacy and safety data, and tolerance and rebound insomnia are described for doxylamine.[1][2]
